name: Small Operations
tags: binary search, brute force, dfs and similar, dp, math, number theory, sortings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0275 DP + GCD OA problem
brief: Turn x into y (<=1e6) by multiplying or dividing (exactly) by integers in [1,k]. Minimum operations or -1.
key_idea: Divide x down to g=gcd(x,y), then multiply up to y; each part needs min #factors (<=k) whose product is x/g (resp. y/g) - DP over divisors.
solution:
1. g = gcd(x,y); need factorizations of X = x/g and Y = y/g.
2. f(m): list divisors of m sorted; dp[d] = min over divisors e of d with d/e <= k of dp[e]+1; dp[1]=0.
3. If f(X) or f(Y) infinite (a prime factor > k) -> -1.
4. Answer f(X)+f(Y).

name: Maximum Subarray
tags: data structures, dp, greedy, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0261 Group knapsack with no adjacent groups
brief: Add x to exactly k positions (k<=20) and subtract x from all others; maximise the max subarray sum (empty = 0). n<=2e5.
key_idea: Kadane with an extra state j = number of +x positions used in the prefix; prefix must be able to split into j pluses and (i+1-j) minuses.
solution:
1. dp[j] = best sum of a subarray ending at i (or 0 = empty/restart) with j pluses among a_0..a_i.
2. dp'[j] = max(0, dp[j] + a_i - x, dp[j-1] + a_i + x).
3. Valid only if j <= i+1 and i+1-j <= n-k (remaining elements can absorb the rest).
4. Answer = max over all valid dp values.
dry_run:
a=2 -1 2 3, k=1, x=2: best is +x on a value inside a long segment.
Choose +2 on 3: array 0 -3 0 5 -> max 5.
Answer 5.

name: Searchlights
tags: binary search, brute force, data structures, dp, implementation, sortings, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0480 Minimum Adjacent Swaps to Group Binary String
brief: n robbers and m searchlights (<=2000 each). A light sees robber if a<=c and b<=d. Each move shifts all robbers right or up by 1. Min moves so no light sees any robber.
key_idea: For each (robber, light) pair with gap x=c-a>=0, if right moves <= x we need up moves >= d-b+1; take suffix maxima over x and minimise x + needed up.
solution:
1. need[x] = max over pairs with c-a = x (and d>=b) of d-b+1.
2. Sweep x from max (1e6+1) down to 0: suf = max(suf, need[x]).
3. With x right moves, required up = suf (all pairs with gap >= x); ans = min(ans, x + suf).
4. Pairs with c<a or d<b never matter.
dry_run:
Robber (0,0), light (2,3): need[2]=4.
x=3: suf=0 -> 3. x=2: suf=4 -> 6.
Answer 3.

name: Pchelyonok and Segments
tags: binary search, data structures, dp, greedy, math
nearest_infosys_question: Q0297 Investment opportunities (non-overlapping range revenue)
brief: Pick max k and k disjoint segments left to right with lengths k, k-1, ..., 1 whose sums strictly increase (a_i ≥ 1, n ≤ 1e5).
key_idea: Go right-to-left: dp[k][i] = max sum of a length-k segment starting at ≥ i that can be followed by a valid chain k-1..1; k ≤ ~447.
solution:
1. Prefix sums p.
2. dp1[i] = max_{j≥i} a_j.
3. dpk[i] = max(dpk[i+1], s(i,i+k-1)) if s(i,i+k-1) < dp(k-1)[i+k]; else dpk[i+1].
4. Answer = largest k with dpk[0] defined; stop when k(k+1)/2 > n.
5. Keep only two layers (rolling arrays).
complexity: O(n sqrt n) time, O(n) space

k=1: dp1[6]=6.
k=2: segment [3,2]=5 at i=4 < dp1[6]=6 -> dp2[0]=5.
k=3: segment [2,1,1]=4 at i=1 < dp2[4]=5 -> ok.
Answer 3 (matches).

name: Factorials and Powers of Two
tags: bitmasks, brute force, constructive algorithms, dp, math
nearest_infosys_question: Q0711 Sudoku Solver
brief: A number is powerful if it is a power of two or a factorial. Given n <= 1e12, find the minimum number of DISTINCT powerful numbers summing to n (or -1).
key_idea: Only factorials 3!..14! (12 of them) are not powers of two; brute-force every subset of them, and cover the remainder with its binary representation (popcount).
solution:
1. Precompute f = {6, 24, ..., 14!} (12 values; 15! > 1e12; 1!,2! are powers of two).
2. For each mask of 4096 subsets: S = sum; if S <= n, candidate = popcount(mask) + popcount(n - S).
3. Answer = min candidate (always exists, so never -1).
4. Distinctness holds: binary bits are distinct powers of two, and none equals a chosen factorial >= 6.

mask {6}: 1 + popcount(5)=1+2=3.
mask {24} too big. Min = 3.
Sample 7: {6} -> 1 + popcount(1) = 2.

name: Living Sequence
tags: binary search, dp, math, number theory
nearest_infosys_question: Q0653 Special Prime Pairs
brief: The sequence of positive integers that do not contain the digit 4: 1,2,3,5,6,... Output the k-th element (k <= 1e12).
key_idea: Numbers without digit 4 are base-9 numbers with digits 0..8 mapped to 0,1,2,3,5,6,7,8,9: write k in base 9 and map digits >= 4 to digit+1.
solution:
1. Convert k to base 9 (least significant first).
2. Map each digit d -> d < 4 ? d : d+1.
3. Read digits from most significant to build the answer (long long).
4. Works because the k-th valid number corresponds to the base-9 representation of k.
complexity: O(log k) per test, O(1) space

name: Make Them Equal
nearest_infosys_question: Q0232 Knapsack with additional constraints
brief: Array starts all 1s. One operation: choose i and x >= 1 and add floor(a_i/x) to a_i. With at most k operations, you earn c_i for each i with a_i = b_i (b_i <= 1000). Maximize coins.
key_idea: Precompute steps[v] = min operations to reach v from 1 (BFS over values <= 1000, at most 12). Then it's a 0/1 knapsack with weight steps[b_i], value c_i, capacity min(k, 12n).
solution:
1. BFS/DP: steps[1] = 0; for v, for x = 1..v: w = v + v/x, if w <= 1000 steps[w] = min(steps[w], steps[v]+1).
2. cap = min(k, sum of steps[b_i]) (capacity beyond that is useless).
3. 0/1 knapsack: for each i, for j = cap..w_i: dp[j] = max(dp[j], dp[j-w_i] + c_i).
4. Answer dp[cap].
complexity: O(1000^2) precompute + O(n * 12n) knapsack, O(12n) space
dry_run:
Sample 1: b = 1 7 5 2, c = 2 6 5 2, k=4. steps: 1->0, 2->1, 5->3 (1,2,4,5), 7->4 (1,2,3,6,7).
Weights 0,4,3,1; capacity 4.
Best: items b=1 (2) + b=5 (5) + b=2 (2) = weight 4, value 9.
Answer 9 (expected 9).

name: Planar Reflections
nearest_infosys_question: Q0205 Count number-line paths with exactly k jumps
brief: n planes in a row and a particle with decay age k. Each plane lets a particle pass and also emits a copy in the opposite direction with age k-1 (age 1 makes no copies). Count all particles produced, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: dp[k][x] = particles generated by one particle of age k with x planes ahead (so n-x behind). Crossing the j-th plane ahead emits an age k-1 particle with (n-x)+(j-1) planes ahead of it: dp[k][x] = 1 + sum_{y=n-x}^{n-1} dp[k-1][y].
solution:
1. dp[1][x] = 1 for all x; dp[k][0] = 1.
2. For age a = 2..k: prefix sums of dp[a-1]; dp[a][x] = 1 + (pre[n] - pre[n-x]).
3. Answer dp[k][n].
4. Keep only two rows; per test O(n*k), sums bounded by 1000.

name: Number of Ways
tags: binary search, brute force, data structures, dp, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0546 Binary array trim to balance
brief: Array of n<=5e5 integers; count the ways to cut it into three contiguous non-empty parts with equal sums.
key_idea: With total S divisible by 3, count pairs of cut points i<j where prefix(i) = S/3 and prefix(j) = 2S/3 (j <= n-1), scanning once with a running counter.
solution:
1. S = total; if S % 3 != 0 answer 0.
2. Scan i = 1..n-1 over prefix sums pre[i].
3. First, if pre[i] == 2S/3, add cnt (number of earlier indices with prefix S/3) to the answer.
4. Then, if pre[i] == S/3, cnt++ (order matters when S = 0 so the middle part is non-empty).
5. Use long long for sums and answer.
dry_run:
Sample 1: a=1 2 3 0 3, S=9, targets 3 and 6.
pre: 1,3,6,6 (i=1..4).
i=2: pre=3 -> cnt=1. i=3: pre=6 -> ans+=1. i=4: pre=6 -> ans+=1.
Answer 2 (matches).

name: Caesar's Legions
nearest_infosys_question: Q0290 1D Minesweeper string fill count
brief: Arrange n1 identical footmen and n2 identical horsemen in a row (n1,n2<=100) so no more than k1 footmen or k2 horsemen stand consecutively (k<=10). Count arrangements mod 1e8.
key_idea: f[i][j][c] = arrangements using i footmen, j horsemen ending with a block of type c; append a whole block of length 1..k of the other type.
solution:
1. f[0][0][0] = f[0][0][1] = 1 (empty start can be followed by either type).
2. f[i][j][0] = sum_{t=1..min(k1,i)} f[i-t][j][1] (last block: t footmen).
3. f[i][j][1] = sum_{t=1..min(k2,j)} f[i][j-t][0].
4. Answer (f[n1][n2][0] + f[n1][n2][1]) mod 1e8.

name: Three Blocks Palindrome (easy version)
tags: binary search, brute force, data structures, dp, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0550 Longest subarray with sum >= 0
brief: Values in 1..26, n<=2000. Find the longest subsequence of the form x copies of a, y copies of b, x copies of a.
key_idea: For outer value a and count x, take its x-th occurrence from the left and from the right; the middle is the most frequent value strictly between them (prefix counts).
solution:
1. pre[v][i] = count of value v in a[0..i).
2. Answer starts with max frequency of any value (x=0).
3. For each value a with positions p[0..c-1], for x=1..c/2: l=p[x-1], r=p[c-x]; mid = max over b of pre[b][r]-pre[b][l+1].
4. Candidate 2x+mid; take max.
complexity: O(26 * n * 26 / 2) worst case, O(26 n) space
dry_run:
Sample 1: 1 1 2 2 3 2 1 1, a=1 positions 0,1,6,7.
x=2: l=1, r=6: between = 2 2 3 2 -> max b=2 count 3.
2*2+3=7 (matches).

name: Bear and Prime Numbers
tags: binary search, brute force, data structures, dp, implementation, math, number theory
nearest_infosys_question: Q0872 K-switching binary string
brief: Given n numbers (<=1e7) and m queries [l,r] (r up to 2e9), output the sum over primes p in [l,r] of the count of numbers divisible by p.
key_idea: Sieve to 1e7; f(p)=sum of cnt[multiples of p]; prefix sums over primes; clamp query ranges to 1e7.
solution:
1. cnt[v] = occurrences of value v.
2. Sieve of Eratosthenes up to 1e7; for each prime p, f(p)=sum cnt[p], cnt[2p], ... (computed while crossing out).
3. pre[i] = sum of f(p) for primes p<=i.
4. Query: clamp r=min(r,1e7), l=min(l,1e7+1); answer pre[r]-pre[l-1] (0 if l>r).
5. Use fast IO for n=1e6.
complexity: O(M log log M) precompute (M=1e7), O(1) per query; ~90MB memory

name: Berry Jam
nearest_infosys_question: Q0546 Binary array trim to balance
brief: 2n jars (1=strawberry, 2=blueberry); Karlsson in the middle repeatedly empties the nearest full jar on the left or right. Minimize jars emptied so remaining full jars have equal counts of both types.
key_idea: Remaining jars = a prefix of the left half plus a suffix of the right half; need balance(prefix)+balance(suffix)=0; hash map of suffix balances to minimal removals.
solution:
1. Balance: +1 for type 1, -1 for type 2.
2. For the right half, for each suffix starting at j (n+1..2n+1), removed = j-(n+1); store in map best[balance] the minimal removed (iterate j from n+1 upward and keep the first).
3. For each prefix length i (0..n) of the left half, removed = n-i; look up best[-bal(prefix i)].
4. Answer = min over i of (n-i)+best[...]. Emptying everything always works (0=0).
complexity: O(n log n) with map (O(n) with an offset array)
dry_run:
Sample 4: n=2, a=2 1 1 1.
Right suffixes: j=3 (1 1): bal 2, rem 0; j=4 (1): bal 1, rem 1; j=5: bal 0, rem 2.
Left prefix i=1 (2): bal -1 -> need 1 -> rem (2-1)+1 = 2; i=0 -> need 0 -> 2+2=4.
Answer 2 (matches).

name: Paint the Tree
tags: brute force, dfs and similar, dp, greedy, shortest paths, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0357 Sum of station costs to reach station 1
brief: Tree, pieces P_A at a (paints white->red) and P_B at b (paints red->blue); each step A moves then B moves. Find the minimum steps to make all vertices blue.
key_idea: B should first meet A's red trail at the midpoint c of path a-b (after ceil(d/2) steps), then do a DFS tour from c: 2(n-1) - (max depth from c).
solution:
1. BFS from a to get parent pointers toward a and d=dist(a,b).
2. t = ceil(d/2) = (d+1)/2; walk t steps from b toward a to get c (vertex B reaches first that is already red).
3. From c, B must visit every vertex; a full tour returning is 2(n-1) steps, ending at the deepest vertex saves maxDist(c).
4. Answer = t + 2(n-1) - maxDist(c) (BFS from c). A always stays ahead painting red.
5. a==b: t=0, c=a.
dry_run:
Sample 1: n=2, a=1, b=2, d=1.
t=1, c=1 (one step from 2 toward 1).
maxDist(1)=1 -> 1 + 2*1 - 1 = 2 (matches).

name: Greenhouse Effect
nearest_infosys_question: Q0244 Special LIS
brief: n plants of m species on a line (given sorted by position). Place borders so section i holds only species i; min plants to move.
key_idea: Kept plants must have non-decreasing species in position order -> answer = n - longest non-decreasing subsequence.
solution:
1. Read species s_1..s_n (positions only matter for order; read x as string/double and ignore).
2. Compute LNDS with tails array and upper_bound (non-strict).
3. Answer n - LNDS length.
4. (O(n*m) DP dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j<i, s_j<=s_i] also fits n<=5000.)
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

name: XOR Equation
nearest_infosys_question: Q0324 Ordinary Numbers (binary string XOR pairs)
brief: Count ordered pairs of positive integers (a,b) with a+b=s and a xor b=x (s,x<=1e12).
key_idea: a+b = (a^b) + 2(a&b): AND is fixed as d=(s-x)/2; each set bit of x can go to a or b freely.
solution:
1. If s<x or (s-x) odd -> 0.
2. d=(s-x)/2; if d & x != 0 -> 0 (a bit can't be both in AND and XOR).
3. ans = 2^popcount(x).
4. If d==0, the pairs (0,x),(x,0) are invalid (need positive) -> ans -= 2.
5. Use 64-bit; popcount via __builtin_popcountll.
dry_run:

popcount(5)=2 -> 4 pairs; d!=0 so no subtraction.
Output 4 ((2,7),(3,6),(6,3),(7,2)).

name: Maximum Distributed Tree
tags: dfs and similar, dp, greedy, implementation, math, number theory, sortings, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0908 Count Trees Similar by Depth Profile
brief: Label tree edges with positive ints whose product is k (given as m primes), minimizing number of 1s; maximize sum over all pairs of path label sums, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: Edge e is used by sz*(n-sz) pairs; pair biggest labels with biggest usage counts.
solution: 1) DFS for subtree sizes; cnt_e = sz*(n-sz) (fits long long). 2) Sort cnt descending, primes descending. 3) If m > n-1: multiply the largest m-(n-1)+1 primes (mod) into one label for the top edge; remaining primes go one per edge. 4) If m <= n-1: assign primes in order, the rest get label 1. 5) Sum (cnt mod P)*label mod P.
complexity: O(n log n + m log m) time

name: Xor-Subsequence (easy version)
tags: bitmasks, brute force, dp, strings, trees, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0304 Longest Special Subsequence (bitwise LIS)
brief: Array a (a_i <= 200). Find the longest subsequence of indices b_0<b_1<... with a[b_p] XOR b_{p+1} < a[b_{p+1}] XOR b_p for each consecutive pair.
key_idea: LIS-style dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j]; because a <= 200 < 256, only j >= i-256 can satisfy the condition (higher bits of i and j would decide it the wrong way).
solution: 1) dp[i]=1. 2) For j from max(0,i-256) to i-1: if (a[j]^i) < (a[i]^j) then dp[i]=max(dp[i], dp[j]+1). 3) Answer = max dp.

name: Cubes
nearest_infosys_question: Q0094 Rotated prefix MEX cost
brief: n cubes with colors; delete at most k cubes. Maximize the longest run of equal colors after deletion.
key_idea: For each color, take a window of its occurrences; cubes to delete = span length - count; two pointers keep that <= k.
solution: 1) pos[c] = list of indices of color c. 2) For each color: i=0; for j over its list: while (pos[j]-pos[i]+1) - (j-i+1) > k: i++. 3) ans = max(ans, j-i+1). 4) Print ans.

name: Mahmoud and Ehab and the xor-MST
nearest_infosys_question: Q0324 Ordinary Numbers (binary string XOR pairs)
brief: Find the MST weight of the complete graph on vertices 0..n-1 (n up to 1e12), where edge (u,v) has weight u XOR v.
key_idea: Connecting each vertex i to i XOR lowbit(i) is optimal. So the MST weight is the sum of lowbit(i) for i=1..n-1, counted bit by bit.
solution:
1. Let N = n-1.
2. For each bit b: the count of i in [1,N] with lowbit 2^b is floor(N/2^b) - floor(N/2^(b+1)).
3. ans += count * 2^b.
4. Use long long; the answer is about 2e13 at most.

b=1: 1-0 = 1 number, contributing 2.
Total 4 (matches).

name: Bookshelves
nearest_infosys_question: Q0138 Maximum Xor-Sum in range [0,K]
brief: Split n<=50 numbers (each < 2^50) into k contiguous non-empty groups so that the AND of the group sums is as large as possible.
key_idea: Build the answer greedily from the high bit down. Try cand = ans|bit, and check with a partition DP whether every group sum can contain all the bits of cand.
solution:
1. Prefix sums P. Go through bits b from 56 down to 0.
2. cand = ans | (1<<b). dp[i][j] = can the first i items form j groups with ((P[i]-P[p]) & cand) == cand for each group.
3. dp[0][0] = true. Transition over every split point p < i.
4. If dp[n][k] is true, set ans = cand.

name: Sub-RBS (Hard Version)
nearest_infosys_question: Q0310 Minesweeper 1D string completion count
brief: Sum the scores of all subsequences of a bracket string (n<=100), mod 998244353. A regular t scores the max length of a regular subsequence of t that is lexicographically 'better' ('(' < ')') than t, or 0 if none.
key_idea: A regular t scores |t|-2 exactly when some ')' is followed later by at least two '('. Delete that ')' (with the '(' after it shifting forward) and one later '('. Otherwise it scores 0. So count the regular subsequences with that property, along with their total length.
solution:
1. State (balance, phase). Phase 0 = no ')' yet, 1 = a ')' seen, 2 = ')' then one '(', 3 = ')' then two '(' (the property holds).
2. A '(' moves phase 0->0, 1->2, 2->3, 3->3. A ')' (only if balance>0) moves phase 0->1 and leaves 1, 2, 3 unchanged.
3. Keep cnt and the sum of lengths. Taking a char adds cnt to the length sum.
4. The answer is L[0][3] - 2*cnt[0][3] mod p.

name: Two Strings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0317 Optimal run-length encoding after deletions
brief: Strings s,t (<=2e5). Is every position of s used by at least one occurrence of t as a subsequence of s? (No if t isn't a subsequence.)
key_idea: Position i with char c is coverable iff some j with t[j]=c has t[0..j-1] matchable in s[0..i-1] and t[j+1..] matchable in s[i+1..].
solution:
1. Greedy prefix match p(i) = how much of t fits in s[0..i-1]; allowed j <= min(p,m-1). L[i] = largest allowed j with t[j]==s[i] (keep last[c] as the allowed range grows).
2. Symmetric from the right: suffix match q; allowed j >= m-1-q; R[i] = smallest allowed j with t[j]==s[i].
3. i is covered iff L[i] exists and L[i] >= R[i].
4. Any uncovered i -> No (also covers t not a subsequence).

s=abacaba, t=aba.
i=3 ('c'): no j with t[j]='c' -> L=-1 -> No.
s=abab,t=ab: i=0 a: L=0,R=0 ok; i=1 b: L=1,R=1; i=2 a: L=0,R=0; i=3 b ok -> Yes.

name: Chip Move
nearest_infosys_question: Q0239 Count K-element Selections with Sum at most M
brief: Chip at 0; the i-th move length must be a positive multiple of k+i-1. For every x in 1..n (<=2e5) count ways to reach x mod 998244353.
key_idea: Number of moves is O(sqrt n) since the minimum distance after j moves is k+(k+1)+...; per move do an unbounded-knapsack style prefix transition.
solution:
1. cur[x] = ways to be at x after j moves (cur[0]=1 initially).
2. Next move with step s: nx[x] = nx[x-s] + cur[x-s] (any multiple of s).
3. ans[x] += nx[x] for every round.
4. Stop when the minimum reachable position exceeds n.
complexity: O(n sqrt n) time, O(n) space

move2 (mult of 2): nx[3]=cur[1]=1, nx[4]=cur[2]=1, nx[5]=nx[3]+cur[3]=2...

name: Little Pony and Harmony Chest
nearest_infosys_question: Q0668 Minimum subset with LCM equal to array LCM
brief: Given a_1..a_n (n<=100, a_i<=30), find pairwise-coprime positive b_i minimising sum |a_i - b_i| (the expression is an image on the page; this is the known objective, consistent with the samples).
key_idea: b_i never needs to exceed 58 (b=1 is always allowed, costs <= 29); only 16 primes < 59 -> dp over (index, mask of used primes).
solution:
1. pm[b] = mask of primes dividing b, for b in 1..58.
2. dp[i][S] = min cost for first i elements using primes S.
3. Transition with b where pm[b] & S == 0: dp[i+1][S|pm[b]] = dp[i][S] + |a_i - b|; store choice.
4. Pick min over S at i=n, backtrack choices.

name: String Coloring (hard version)
nearest_infosys_question: Q0099 Three-person array rearrangement
brief: Colour each character of s (n<=2e5) with the fewest colours so that swapping adjacent differently-coloured characters can sort s.
key_idea: Every pair i<j with s_i > s_j needs different colours; colour c_i = 1 + max colour of earlier strictly larger letters (= longest decreasing subsequence ending at i).
solution:
1. mx[ch] = max colour assigned so far to letter ch.
2. c_i = 1 + max(mx[d] for d > s_i).
3. mx[s_i] = max(mx[s_i], c_i).
4. res = max c_i (length of longest strictly decreasing subsequence).

5. Edges that leave the grid never return, so dropping them is safe. Use two rolling rows.

1. f[1]=1, prefix S[x]=f[1]+..+f[x].
2. For x=2..n: f[x] = S[x-1] + sum over blocks of z with same q=x/z: (z_hi - z_lo + 1) * f[q], where z_hi = x/q.
3. Update S[x]. All mod m (use long long).
4. Answer f[n].
complexity: O(n sqrt n) time, O(n) space

name: Ranom Numbers
tags: brute force, dp, greedy, math, strings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0281 Array Minimization Game
brief: String over A..E with values 1,10,100,1000,10000; a digit counts negative if some digit to its right is strictly larger, else positive. Change at most one character to maximize the total.
key_idea: Signs depend only on the max to the right: precompute suffix value/max, and prefix value as a function of the max coming from the right (5 states).
solution: 1) R[i] = value of s[i..] alone, M[i] = max letter in s[i..] (computed right to left). 2) P[i][m] = value of s[0..i-1] given the max to its right is m: P[i+1][m] = P[i][max(m,s_i)] + (s_i>=m ? +val(s_i) : -val(s_i)). 3) For each i and each letter c: total = P[i][max(c,M[i+1])] + (c>=M[i+1] ? val(c) : -val(c)) + R[i+1]. 4) Answer = max (includes c = s_i, i.e. no change).
complexity: O(25 n) time, O(5 n) space
dry_run: Sample 'AB' (A=0,B=1 indices): original -1+10=9. Change A->E at i=0: P=0, M[1]=B, E>=B -> +10000, R[1]=10 -> 10010. Best 10010.

name: Escape The Maze (hard version)
tags: dfs and similar, dp, greedy, shortest paths, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0912 Min vertex removals so every tree component has < K vertices
brief: Vlad starts at root 1 of a tree and wants to reach a leaf. Friends start at given vertices and want to meet him first. Find the minimum number of friends that guarantees a catch, or -1 if he always escapes.
key_idea: A friend can block vertex v if dist_friend(v) <= depth(v). Going down from the root, the first blockable vertex on a path needs exactly one friend (the nearest one). If any leaf can be reached without passing a blockable vertex, the answer is -1.
solution:
1. Run a multi-source BFS from the friends to get df[]. Run a BFS from 1 to get depth d[] and the parents.
2. In reverse BFS order: if v != 1 and df[v] <= d[v], then res[v]=1 (the cut). Else if v is a leaf, mark it bad (Vlad escapes).
3. Otherwise res[v] = sum of the children's res, and v is bad if any child is bad.
4. Output -1 if the root is bad, else res[1].
dry_run:

d[2]=1 and df[2]=0 <= 1, so vertex 2 is a cut with res=1.
The root sums to 1, so the answer is 1 (matches). All 4 samples were verified.

name: Koa and the Beach (Easy Version)
nearest_infosys_question: Q0378 Longest increasing path in matrix
brief: Koa swims from the shore (0) to the island (n+1). Each second she moves forward by one or stays. The tide p cycles 0,1,..,k,..,1 with period 2k, and at every integer time her depth d_x+p[t mod 2k] must be <= l. Can she reach the island? n,k <= 100.
key_idea: The state (position, time mod 2k) captures everything, so BFS over at most 101*200 states.
solution:
1. Build p: p[i]=i for i<=k, and p[i]=2k-i for i>k.
2. Start the BFS at (0,0). The shore is always safe.
3. From (x,t): the next time is t'=(t+1)%2k, and you can go to x'=x or x+1. If x'==n+1, answer Yes. If x'==0, or 1<=x'<=n with d[x']+p[t']<=l, push the state if it is unvisited.
4. If the BFS ends without reaching the island, answer No.

Wait on the shore (t=1). At t=2 (p=0) move to x=1 with depth 1 <= 1. At t=3 (p=1) move to x=2 with depth 0+1 = 1. At t=4 reach x=3, the island.
Yes (matches).

name: Palindrome
nearest_infosys_question: Q0269 Matrix Chain Multiplication Variant
brief: String s (n<=5e4). Print a palindromic subsequence of length exactly 100 if one exists, else the longest palindromic subsequence.
key_idea: If n>=2600 some letter occurs >=100 times (pigeonhole); otherwise n is small enough for O(n^2) LPS DP.
solution:
1. If any letter occurs >=100 times, print it 100 times.
2. Else n<2600: d[i][j]=LPS of s[i..j]; d[i][j]=d[i+1][j-1]+2 if s[i]==s[j], else max(d[i+1][j],d[i][j-1]).
3. Reconstruct: walk i,j inward collecting matched left half L and optional middle char.
4. Palindrome = L+mid+rev(L). If longer than 100, take first 50 of L and mirror it (still a subsequence).
5. Use short ints for the 2600^2 table (memory).
complexity: O(n^2) time and space for n<2600, else O(n)

name: Ultra-Meow
nearest_infosys_question: Q0154 The Oracle of Eldoria
brief: For a = {1..n}, sum over all subsets b of MEX(b, |b|+1) (the (|b|+1)-th positive integer missing from b), mod 1e9+7. n ≤ 5000, sum n^2 ≤ 2.5e7.
key_idea: Fix size k and the value m of the answer: m missing and exactly k missing numbers below m fixes how many of b lie below m.
solution:
1. Precompute Pascal C up to 5000.
2. For each k and m in [k+1, min(n, 2k+1)]: j = m-1-k elements of b are < m, rest > m.
3. Count = C(m-1, j) * C(n-m, k-j); add m*count.
4. If 2k+1 > n, subsets where answer exceeds n give exactly 2k+1: add (2k+1)*C(n,k).
5. Sum mod 1e9+7.

name: Doremy's Pegging Game
nearest_infosys_question: Q0154 The Oracle of Eldoria
brief: n pegs on a regular n-gon around a central peg; remove pegs one by one (append to array) until the band touches the centre. Count distinct removal arrays mod p (n<=5000).
key_idea: The band touches the centre exactly when some run of consecutive removed pegs reaches t = floor(n/2). Fix the last removed peg; it joins x left and y right removed pegs (x,y <= t-1, x+y+1 >= t); other pegs outside the run can be removed freely.
solution:
1. t = n/2. Multiply the answer by n (rotation symmetry for the last peg).
2. For s = x+y from t-1 to n-2: pairs(s) = #(x,y) with 0<=x,y<=t-1, x+y=s.
3. Free pegs m = max(0, n-s-3) (excluding the two pegs bounding the run); choose k of them removed earlier: C(m,k) * (s+k)! orders.
4. ans += pairs(s) * sum_k C(m,k)(s+k)!.
5. Runs among free pegs can't reach t (they're too short).
dry_run:
n=4, t=2: s=1: 2 pairs, m=0 -> 1! -> 2. s=2: 1 pair (1,1), m=0 -> 2! = 2.
Per last peg 4; times n=4 -> 16.
Matches sample.

brief: Colour each element white or black to minimize seg(white subsequence) + seg(black subsequence), where seg counts the elements left after merging equal neighbours.
key_idea: Keep the last values x and y of the two subsequences. If a_i equals either one, append it there for free. Otherwise pay 1 and overwrite the tail whose value reappears later (or never), keeping the one needed sooner (Belady-style).
solution:
1. Precompute the occurrence lists so nextOcc(v,i) can be found by binary search. Empty tails get INF.
2. x=y=0, ans=0.
3. If a_i==x or a_i==y, skip. Else ans++. If nextOcc(x) < nextOcc(y), set y=a_i; else x=a_i.
4. Print ans.

name: How Many Paths?
tags: dfs and similar, dp, graphs, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0381 Graph + DP OA problem
brief: For each vertex v of a directed graph (self-loops allowed), output whether the number of paths from vertex 1 to v is 0, 1, more than 1 but finite (2), or infinite (-1).
key_idea: Run an iterative DFS from 1. An edge to a gray vertex means that vertex is on a reachable cycle, so mark it infinite. An edge to a black vertex means that vertex is reached twice, so mark it '2'. Spread each mark to everything reachable from it, with -1 overriding 2.
solution:
1. Iterative DFS with colors 0 (white), 1 (gray), 2 (black).
2. Edge to white: push it. Edge to gray: inf[v]=1. Edge to black: two[v]=1.
3. BFS-spread the inf marks along the edges, then the two marks.
4. Output: unreached gives 0, inf gives -1, two gives 2, else 1.

name: Sum over all Substrings (Hard Version)
tags: bitmasks, divide and conquer, dp, dsu, greedy, implementation, strings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0281 Array Minimization Game
brief: Sum over all substrings of a binary string of f(substring). f(t) is the minimum number of ones in a string p such that every '1' of t has a window [i-1,i+1] in p containing more 1s than 0s.
key_idea: For one string, the greedy is: at the first uncovered '1' at position i, place a 1 at i+1, which covers i..i+2, then jump to i+3. Summing over all substrings that start at i gives g[i] = g[i+1] if s_i=='0', else (n-i)+g[i+3].
solution:
1. Use 0-indexed positions, with g[n]=g[n+1]=g[n+2]=0.
2. For i from n-1 down to 0: if s[i]=='0', g[i]=g[i+1]. Otherwise g[i]=(n-i)+g[i+3], since every substring starting at i that reaches past i pays 1, and the rest continues from i+3.
3. Answer = sum of g[i]. Use long long.
dry_run:
s='1': g[0]=1, answer 1.
s='10': g[0]=2, g[1]=0, answer 2.
Sample outputs 1 2 0 346 match.

name: Red-Black Number
tags: dfs and similar, dp, implementation, math, meet-in-the-middle
nearest_infosys_question: Q0279 Last Stone Weight II with adjacency bonus R
brief: Color each of n <= 40 digits red or black so the red number is divisible by A, the black by B (A,B <= 40), both colors used; minimize |#red - #black|, print a coloring or -1.
key_idea: Reachability DP over (digit index, red mod A, black mod B, red count) with backtracking.
solution:
1. vis[i][ra][rb][r]: after i digits, red value mod A, black mod B, r reds is reachable.
2. Digit d: red -> ra' = (10ra+d)%A, r+1; black -> rb' = (10rb+d)%B.
3. Pick r in [1,n-1] with vis[n][0][0][r] minimizing |n-2r|; none -> -1.
4. Backtrack from the end: find a predecessor mod value that leads to the current state.
complexity: O(n^2 * A * B) time and space (~2.6e6 states)

name: Vlad and the Nice Paths (easy version)
nearest_infosys_question: Q0154 The Oracle of Eldoria
brief: n <= 100 colored tiles; a path picks increasing indices; it is nice if its length is a multiple of k and each consecutive block of k tiles has one color. Count nice paths of maximum length mod 1e9+7 (empty path counts).
key_idea: dp[i] = (max blocks, count) for paths whose last block ends at tile i; the block picks k-1 more tiles of color c_i between the previous end j and i: C(cnt, k-1) ways.
solution:
1. State 0 = empty path (len 0, count 1).
2. For each i, scan j = i-1 down to 0 keeping same = #tiles of color c_i in (j, i).
3. If same >= k-1: candidate len[j]+1 with ways cnt[j]*C(same, k-1); keep max len, sum counts on ties.
4. Answer = sum of cnt[i] over states (including 0) with the overall max len.
complexity: O(n^2) per test, O(n^2) for binomials

name: Assimilation IV
tags: combinatorics, dp, math, probabilities, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0338 Great Ball Chains
brief: n <= 20 cities built one per turn in random order; a monument built at turn t has range n-t+1 at the end. m <= 5e4 points with distances d(i,j). Expected number of points controlled, mod 998244353.
key_idea: Linearity of expectation; a point is missed iff each city i is built in one of the last d_ij - 1 turns; count such permutations by sorting the allowed sizes.
solution:
1. For point j, city i fails to cover it iff built at turn > n+1-d, i.e. in the last s_i = d_ij - 1 turns.
2. Sort s ascending; #bad permutations = prod over i (0-based) of max(0, s_i - i).
3. P(conquered) = 1 - bad/n!.
4. Sum over points mod p using inverse of n!.
complexity: O(m * n log n) time, O(nm) space

name: Compress String
nearest_infosys_question: Q0317 Optimal run-length encoding after deletions
brief: Split string s (n <= 5000) into pieces; a single character costs a, a piece that already occurs as a substring of the concatenation before it costs b. Minimize total cost.
key_idea: dp over prefixes plus an LCP table: mx[j] = longest piece starting at j that occurs completely inside s[0..j) = max over k<j of min(lcp(k,j), j-k).
solution:
1. lcp[k][j] = s[k]==s[j] ? lcp[k+1][j+1]+1 : 0; compute row by row (k descending) with two 1D arrays.
2. mx[j] = max over k<j of min(lcp[k][j], j-k) (the occurrence must end before j).
3. dp[0]=0; dp[j+1] = min(dp[j+1], dp[j]+a); for i in (j, j+mx[j]]: dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[j]+b).
4. Answer dp[n].

name: Constants in the language of Shakespeare
nearest_infosys_question: Q0138 Maximum Xor-Sum in range [0,K]
brief: Given n in binary (up to 1e6 bits), write n as a sum of the fewest signed powers of two (+-2^x), and print them.
key_idea: The non-adjacent form (NAF) is minimal. Scan from the LSB with a carry; at an odd remainder emit +2^i if the next bit is 0, else -2^i and carry 1.
solution:
1. Reverse the string so index i is bit i. carry c=0.
2. x = bit_i + c. If x==0: c=0. If x==2: c=1 (digit 0).
3. If x==1: if bit_{i+1}==1, emit -2^i and set c=1 (n mod 4 == 3); else emit +2^i and set c=0.
4. Continue two positions past the end to flush the carry. Print the count, then the terms.

name: Send the Fool Further! (medium)
nearest_infosys_question: Q0917 Count tree colorings with B nodes at distance >= K
brief: Tree with edge costs. Heidi starts at node 0 and visits each node at most k times (the first visit counts); each edge is paid only the first time. Maximise the total paid in a worst-case walk.
key_idea: At a node v you can come back from at most k-1 children (each return uses a visit), plus descend into one more child without returning. dp0 = must return to the parent, dp1 = the walk may end inside.
solution:
1. Root at 0. For a child c with edge w: a_c = dp0[c]+w (go and return), b_c = dp1[c]+w (go and end there).
2. dp0[v] = sum of the top (k-1) a_c values.
3. dp1[v] = max(dp0[v], max over c of b_c + the best k-1 a-values among the other children). If c is in the top k-1, use topK - a_c; else use topK-1.
4. The answer is dp1[0].
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

name: Clear the Multiset
tags: data structures, divide and conquer, dp, greedy
nearest_infosys_question: Q0326 Minimum cost to zero an array
brief: Values 1..n with multiplicities a_i (n<=5000). One operation removes one copy of every value in a range with all values present, or removes any number of copies of a single value. Find the minimum number of operations.
key_idea: Divide and conquer: on segment [l,r] (with 'base' already removed by outer ranges), either delete each value individually (r-l+1 ops), or apply (min - base) range ops and recurse on the pieces between the minima.
solution:
1. solve(l,r,base): if l>r return 0.
2. mn = min a[l..r]. option2 = (mn - base) + sum of solve(piece, mn) over the maximal pieces with a > mn.
3. Return min(r-l+1, option2).
4. The answer is solve(0, n-1, 0).

name: Minimal Segment Cover
tags: data structures, dfs and similar, divide and conquer, dp, greedy, implementation, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0253 Distribute wealth to warehouses
brief: n intervals and m queries [x,y] (coordinates <= 5e5). For each query, find the min number of intervals covering [x,y] continuously, or -1.
key_idea: Greedy: from point x jump to the farthest right end reachable by an interval with l<=x. Binary lifting on this jump function answers each query in O(log).
solution:
1. up0[x] = max(x, max r over intervals with l<=x), built as a prefix max over coordinates.
2. up[k][x] = up[k-1][up[k-1][x]] for k<20.
3. Query: from x, for k descending, if up[k][x] < y then jump and add 2^k.
4. If up0[x] >= y the answer is count+1, else -1 (stuck at a gap).
complexity: O((C + m) log C) time with C=5e5, O(C log C) space

name: Travelling Salesman Problem
tags: binary search, data structures, dp, greedy, shortest paths, sortings, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0488 Machine Cooling and Task Scheduling
brief: Visit all n cities starting and ending at city 1. A flight i->j costs max(c_i, a_j - a_i). Minimise the total. n<=1e5.
key_idea: Every city pays at least c_i once (when leaving it). Going down in beauty is free beyond c, so only the uncovered gaps when climbing in sorted order cost extra: total = sum c_i + sum of gaps beyond the running max of (a_i + c_i).
solution:
1. ans = sum of c_i.
2. Sort by a. reach = a_0 + c_0.
3. For i=1..n-1: if a_i > reach, add a_i - reach. Then reach = max(reach, a_i + c_i).
4. Print ans.

name: Bear and Tower of Cubes
nearest_infosys_question: Q0326 Minimum cost to zero an array
brief: Choose X <= m (m <= 1e15); a tower is built greedily by repeatedly adding the largest cube that keeps the volume <= X. Maximize the number of cubes, then X.
key_idea: For remaining limit m with a = floor(cbrt(m)), only two first choices matter: take a^3 (limit m - a^3) or take (a-1)^3 with limit a^3 - 1 - (a-1)^3.
solution:
1. rec(m, cnt, used): if m == 0 record (cnt, used).
2. a = integer cube root of m (fix floating error with while loops).
3. Branch 1: rec(m - a^3, cnt+1, used + a^3).
4. Branch 2 (a > 1): rec(a^3 - 1 - (a-1)^3, cnt+1, used + (a-1)^3).
5. Keep the lexicographically largest (cnt, used); depth is small (limits shrink fast).
complexity: About O(m^(1/3)) branching overall in practice (tiny), O(depth) stack

name: Vitaly and Advanced Useless Algorithms
nearest_infosys_question: Q0278 Machine subset with stability < position
brief: n tasks with non-decreasing deadlines; m options (task e, time t, +p%) each usable once and executed sequentially. Output an order of options finishing every task (>= 100%) by its deadline, or -1.
key_idea: Do tasks in deadline order; for each task independently pick the minimum-time subset reaching 100% with a 0/1 knapsack capped at 100 percent, then check cumulative time.
solution:
1. Group options by task.
2. For task i: dp[j][p] = min time with first j options reaching p% (p capped at 100).
3. If dp[c][100] infinite or time + dp > a_i -> -1.
4. Reconstruct chosen options from the table, append, time += dp[c][100].
5. Print all chosen indices (task by task).
complexity: O(100 * m) time, O(100 * m) space

name: Valera and Fools
tags: dfs and similar, dp, graphs, shortest paths
nearest_infosys_question: Q0381 Graph + DP OA problem
brief: n <= 3000 fools with k <= 3000 rounds. Each round every living fool shoots the smallest-numbered other living fool, and fool i hits with probability p_i%. Count the distinct sets of living fools that are possible after some j <= k rounds.
key_idea: Everyone shoots the smallest fool, and the smallest shoots the second smallest, so the alive set is always {i} U {j..n}. State (i, j). From the suffix j..n, 'i can die' = some p > 0 and 'i can survive' = no p = 100; j can die iff p_i > 0 and survive iff p_i < 100. BFS with depth <= k.
solution:
1. Precompute suffix flags anyPos[j] and any100[j].
2. BFS from (1,2); count every visited state.
3. Expand only if j <= n and dist < k.
4. Transitions: (j, j+1) if i dies and j survives; (i, j+1) if i survives and j dies; (j+1, j+2) if both die (cap the indices at n+1, n+2).

name: Game on Permutation
nearest_infosys_question: Q0498 Make Equal Elements Adjacent (min adjacent swaps)
brief: Permutation game: Alice places a chip, then players alternately (Bob first) move it to a smaller value strictly to the left; a player who cannot move wins. Count starting positions where Alice wins.
key_idea: Position i is lucky iff it is not a prefix minimum (else Bob can't move and wins) and no lucky element to its left has a smaller value (else Bob moves there and wins).
solution:
1. mn = prefix minimum so far, ml = min value among lucky elements so far (INF).
2. For each p_i: lucky if mn < p_i and p_i < ml.
3. If lucky: ans++, ml=p_i.
4. mn=min(mn,p_i).

name: Tetrahedron
nearest_infosys_question: Q0208 Number of handshakes (DP)
brief: An ant on a tetrahedron ABCD starts at D and moves along an edge each step. Count walks of exactly n steps (n <= 1e7) that end at D, modulo 1e9+7.
key_idea: Two states: d = ways to be at D, o = ways to be at one particular other vertex. d' = 3o, o' = d + 2o.
solution:
1. d = 1, o = 0 at step 0.
2. Repeat n times: nd = 3*o mod p; no = (d + 2*o) mod p.
3. Answer d after n steps.
4. O(1) memory (n up to 1e7). Closed form also exists: (3^n + 3*(-1)^n)/4.

nearest_infosys_question: Q0307 Powers of 2 and 5 subset product 10^z
brief: Schedule n competitions in m days (<=5000): competition i has k_i stages every t_i (1 or 2) days; no day holds two stages. Print start days or -1.
key_idea: Pack all t=1 competitions consecutively at the end; the free prefix of length L has (L+1)/2 odd and L/2 even days, and each t=2 competition sits entirely on one parity, so it's a subset-sum split.
solution:
1. S1 = sum k_i for t=1; if S1 > m -> -1. Place them back-to-back starting at day L+1 (L = m - S1).
2. Subset sum over t=2 items: find odd-group sum s <= (L+1)/2 with total - s <= L/2.
3. Reconstruct; place odd group on days 1,3,5,... consecutively, even group on 2,4,6,....
4. None -> -1. (Brute-force checked on small random cases.)
dry_run:
n=2,m=5: (2,1) uses days 4,5; L=3: odd days {1,3}, even {2}.
(2,2) needs 2 days of one parity -> odd: start 1.
Output 4 1.

name: Pokémon Army (hard version)
tags: data structures, divide and conquer, dp, greedy, implementation
nearest_infosys_question: Q0478 Battery charge to make array strictly increasing
brief: Find the maximum alternating sum a_b1 - a_b2 + a_b3 - ... over subsequences. It must be reported initially and after each of q position swaps.
key_idea: The optimum is the sum of max(0, a_i - a_{i+1}) for i=1..n, with a_{n+1}=0: take every local max and min. A swap changes only the terms at indices l-1, l, r-1 and r.
solution:
1. f(i) = max(0, a_i - a_{i+1}) for 1<=i<=n, with a_{n+1}=0.
2. ans = sum of f(i).
3. For a swap (l,r): S = the distinct set {l-1,l,r-1,r}. Subtract f over S, swap, then add f over S back.
4. Print after each step.
dry_run:
Sample 1, 1 3 2: f = 0, 1, 2, so 3.
Swap positions 1 and 2 to get 3 1 2: f = 2, 0, 2, so 4.
Output 3, 4 (matches). All 11 sample outputs were verified.

name: Shovels Shop
nearest_infosys_question: Q0296 Hotel customers minimum unhappiness (Chef Monocarp)
brief: Buy exactly k of the n shovels in purchases. An offer (x,y) makes the y cheapest of x shovels in one purchase free. Minimize the cost (k<=2000).
key_idea: Only the k cheapest shovels matter, bought as consecutive blocks of the sorted order. dp[i] = min over x of dp[i-x] + (the cost of block (i-x, i] minus its best[x] cheapest).
solution:
1. Sort and keep the k cheapest. Prefix sums P.
2. best[x] = max y over the offers with that x (only x<=k matters).
3. dp[i] = min over x=1..i of dp[i-x] + P[i] - P[i-x+best[x]].
4. The answer is dp[k].

Blocks: [1] costs 1, [2,2] costs 2 (one free), [3,4] costs 4. Total 7 (matches).

name: New Year's Puzzle
tags: brute force, dp, graph matchings, greedy, sortings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0064 Insert Interval
brief: Can the free cells of a 2 x n strip (n up to 1e9, m<=2e5 blocked cells) be tiled with dominoes?
key_idea: Sort the blocked cells by column. A fully blocked column acts like a wall. Single blocked cells must pair up consecutively: the region between a pair is tileable iff (same row and odd column distance) or (different rows and even distance). A wall while one cell is pending means NO.
solution:
1. Sort the cells by (column, row).
2. A column with both cells blocked: if a cell is pending, NO; otherwise skip it.
3. A single blocked cell: if nothing is pending, store it. Otherwise check the parity rule against the pending cell, then clear it.
4. If a cell is still pending at the end, NO. Otherwise YES.

name: Turtle Mission: Robot and the Earthquake
tags: dfs and similar, dp, graphs, shortest paths
nearest_infosys_question: Q0378 Longest increasing path in matrix
brief: A robot starts at (0,0) on a cyclic n×m grid of rocks, and the rocks shift up by one each second. It can move down, right or stay. Find the minimum time to reach (n-1,m-1) without colliding, or -1.
key_idea: Work in the rocks' frame. There, 'stay' is useless, 'down' moves 2 rows and needs both cells free, and 'right' moves to (x+1,y+1). BFS finds the earliest time T to reach each cell of the last column. After that you wrap vertically to the real target in min(dd, n-dd) more moves.
solution:
1. BFS on (x mod n, y) in the rock frame. Down goes to (x+2,y) and needs (x+1,y) and (x+2,y) free. Right goes to (x+1,y+1) and needs that cell free.
2. For each row r in column m-1 with BFS time T: real=(r-T) mod n, dd=((n-1)-real) mod n.
3. ans = min of T + min(dd, n-dd). Print -1 if no cell is reachable.
dry_run: Sample 1 gives 7, and the full sample output 7 3 3 8 -1 12 matches.

name: Destroy it!
nearest_infosys_question: Q0066 Stock buy/sell with parity rule
brief: n turns, each with cards (cost 1-3, damage). Each turn play cards with total cost <= 3; every 10th card played overall deals double damage. Maximize total damage.
key_idea: dp[j] = best damage with (cards played) mod 10 = j; per turn only 0-3 cards and a few best combos matter; if the turn crosses a multiple of 10, double the max card of the combo.
solution:
1. Per turn sort cards by cost group descending damage.
2. Options: 1 card = best of each cost; 2 cards = top two cost-1 or top cost-1 + top cost-2; 3 cards = top three cost-1. Store (sum, max).
3. For each j and option with cnt cards: new = dp[j] + sum + (j+cnt >= 10 ? max : 0) -> nd[(j+cnt)%10].
4. Also allow playing nothing. Answer max dp. Use long long.
complexity: O(sum k log k + n*10*6) time, O(k) space

Turn 5: j=9, cnt=1 crosses 10 -> 100 doubled = 200.
Total 263 (matches).

name: Vanya and Brackets
tags: brute force, dp, expression parsing, greedy, implementation, strings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0478 Battery charge to make array strictly increasing
brief: Expression of digits joined by + and * (length <= 5001, at most 15 '*'). Add one pair of brackets to maximise its value.
key_idea: An optimal bracket opens at the start or right after a '*', and closes at the end or right before a '*'. That leaves at most 17^2 candidates, each evaluated in O(n).
solution:
1. Parse into numbers num[0..k-1] and ops.
2. Candidate left ends: 0 and i+1 for each '*' at op i. Candidate right ends: k-1 and i for each '*' at op i.
3. For each l<r: evaluate the inner part, replace it with its value, and evaluate the whole with sum-of-products.
4. Take the max (and also the value with no useful bracket). Use long long; the worst case is about 4.6e18.

name: Balanced Tree
tags: dfs and similar, dp, graphs, greedy, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0912 Min vertex removals so every tree component has < K vertices
brief: Tree nodes with ranges [l_i,r_i]. Choose a_i in its range; an operation (u,v) adds 1 to the subtree of v when rooted at u. Make all values equal and minimise the final value. Sum n <= 2e5.
key_idea: Root at 1. Each edge costs max(0, a_child - a_parent) increments of the whole tree. Choose a_v = clamp(max of the children's a, l_v, r_v) bottom-up; the answer is a_1 + the sum of the positive child-parent differences.
solution:
1. Root at 1 and process nodes in reverse BFS order.
2. a_v = min(r_v, max(l_v, max over children a_c)) (raising a parent is free up to r; a lower parent costs per edge).
3. ans = a_1 + sum over non-root v of max(0, a_v - a_parent(v)).
4. Use long long (values up to ~2e14).

Node 1 has children 2 (6) and 3 (0): a1 = min(11, 6) = 6.
ans = 6 + max(0,6-6) + max(0,0-6) + max(0,5-0) = 11.

name: Max Plus Min Plus Size
tags: data structures, dp, dsu, greedy, implementation, matrices, sortings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0366 Kruskal's minimum spanning tree
brief: Color some non-adjacent elements red; score = max red + min red + number of red. Maximize (n <= 2e5).
key_idea: Some optimal solution contains a global maximum M; sweep the minimum threshold downward activating elements, and with DSU segments count sum ceil(len/2), minus 1 if no segment can include an M while taking ceil(len/2).
solution:
1. Sort indices by value descending; activate them one by one (whole groups of equal values).
2. DSU over active consecutive runs: store start, length, and whether it contains an M at even/odd absolute index.
3. Segment is 'good' if even length and has any M, or odd length and has an M at the start's parity.
4. After activating all values >= v: cnt = sum ceil(len/2); score = M + v + cnt - (no good segment ? 1 : 0).
5. Answer is the maximum over thresholds.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

Threshold 5: segment [1], good, cnt 1 -> 5+5+1 = 11.
Threshold 4: segment [0..2] odd, M at index 1 (wrong parity) -> cnt 2-1 = 1 -> 5+4+1 = 10.

name: Hamiltonian Spanning Tree
tags: dfs and similar, dp, graph matchings, greedy, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0912 Min vertex removals so every tree component has < K vertices
brief: Complete graph on n cities; edges of a given spanning tree cost x, all others cost y. Find the cheapest Hamiltonian path.
key_idea: If x < y maximize tree edges used = maximum vertex-disjoint path cover of the tree (greedy: each vertex links up to 2 children that still have a free end); if x >= y avoid tree edges entirely unless the tree is a star.
solution:
1. x >= y: if some vertex has degree n-1 (star) answer (n-2)*y + x, else (n-1)*y.
2. x < y: process vertices bottom-up; take = min(2, #children with a free end); used += take; v has a free end iff take < 2.
3. Answer used*x + (n-1-used)*y. Use long long.

Vertex 3 links 4 and 5 (take 2, no free end); vertex 1 links 2 only -> used = 3.
Answer 3*2 + 1*3 = 9 (matches); sample 2 (x >= y, not a star) -> 4*2 = 8.

name: Hossam and Friends

nearest_infosys_question: Q0945 Smallest subarray with K good pairs
brief: n people in a line and m pairs who don't know each other; count contiguous segments [a,b] containing no such pair.
key_idea: For each right end r, the left end must exceed the largest x among pairs (x<y) with y<=r.
solution:
1. Normalize each pair so x<y; lim[y]=max(lim[y],x).
2. Sweep r=1..n: cur=max(cur,lim[r]).
3. Segments ending at r: r-cur (left ends cur+1..r).
4. Sum in long long.

name: Vampiric Powers, anyone?
nearest_infosys_question: Q0142 Max Prefix-XOR Sum of Cyclic Traversal
brief: Array a (values < 256). Operation: append XOR of a suffix a_i..a_m. Find the maximum value achievable.
key_idea: Every reachable value is the XOR of some subarray of the original array, so answer = max subarray XOR = max over pairs of prefix XORs.
solution:
1. Keep seen[256] of prefix XORs, seen[0]=true.
2. For each prefix p: for v in 0..255 with seen[v]: ans=max(ans,p^v); then seen[p]=true.
3. Values are < 2^8, so 256 per element.
4. Print ans.

name: Stay or Mirror
tags: brute force, data structures, dp, greedy, sortings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0498 Make Equal Elements Adjacent (min adjacent swaps)
brief: Permutation p of length n (sum n <= 5000). For each i choose a_i = p_i or a_i = 2n - p_i. Minimize the number of inversions of a.
key_idea: For a pair of values x < y, only the smaller value's choice matters: keeping x makes it an inversion iff y is before x; mirroring x makes it an inversion iff y is after x. So each element independently picks min(#larger before, #larger after).
solution:
1. For each i: before = #j < i with p_j > p_i, after = #j > i with p_j > p_i.
2. Answer = sum of min(before, after).
3. O(n^2) is fine (sum n <= 5000); a BIT gives O(n log n).

name: Hungry Games
nearest_infosys_question: Q0272 Highway amplifier coverage
brief: Mushrooms with toxicity a_i and limit x. Eating a segment left to right, g += a_i and if g > x then g resets to 0. Count segments [l, r] whose final g is nonzero.
key_idea: From l, let r be the first index where sum(l..r) > x: segments ending before r are good (r - l of them), at r g resets to 0 and the process restarts at r+1, so dp[l] = (r - l) + dp[r+1].
solution:
1. Prefix sums P (long long).
2. For l = n-1 down to 0: r = first index with P[r+1] - P[l] > x (upper_bound on P).
3. If none: dp[l] = n - l; else dp[l] = (r - l) + dp[r+1] (dp[n] = 0).
4. Answer = sum of dp[l].
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

dp[1]: sum exceeds at r=3 -> 2 + dp[4]=0 -> 2; dp[0]: r=2 -> 2 + dp[3] = 3.
Total 1+2+2+3 = 8 (expected 8).

name: Sum of LDS
tags: brute force, combinatorics, dp, greedy, math
nearest_infosys_question: Q0507 Song volume coefficient changes
brief: Permutation p with max(p_i, p_{i+1}) > p_{i+2} for all i (n <= 5e5). Output the sum, over all subarrays, of the length of the longest decreasing subsequence.
key_idea: Under the condition, LDS of a subarray = its length minus the number of ascents (p_i < p_{i+1}) inside it. So answer = sum of all subarray lengths - sum over ascents at i of i*(n-i) (subarrays containing both i and i+1).
solution:
1. total = sum over lengths: sum_{i=1..n} i*(n-i+1).
2. For each i (1-indexed) with p_i < p_{i+1}: total -= i*(n-i).
3. Print total (long long; ~2e16).
4. Why: greedily take every element except the smaller one of each ascent; the condition guarantees the rest is decreasing.

name: Greg and Graph
nearest_infosys_question: Q0369 Shortest path (Dijkstra then DP variant)
brief: Complete weighted directed graph on n<=500 vertices; vertices are deleted in a given order. Before each deletion output the sum of shortest-path distances over all ordered pairs of remaining vertices.
key_idea: Reverse the process: add vertices in reverse order and run the Floyd-Warshall relaxation with the newly added vertex as the intermediate k; sum over added vertices after each addition.
solution:
1. Read matrix d and order x; process idx = n-1 down to 0 with k = x[idx].
2. Relax all pairs (i, j) (all vertices, not only added): d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]).
3. Mark k added; ans[idx] = sum of d[i][j] over added i, j.
4. Correct because after adding a set of vertices, d holds shortest paths using only added vertices as intermediates.
5. Print ans[0..n-1]; use 64-bit sums.

name: Substring
nearest_infosys_question: Q0379 Min-K Longest Path in DAG
brief: Directed graph with a letter on each node; a path's value is the count of its most frequent letter. Output the maximum path value, or -1 if unbounded (cycle).
key_idea: If there's a cycle the answer is -1; otherwise dp[v][c] = max count of letter c on a path ending at v, in topological order.
solution:
1. Kahn's algorithm; if fewer than n nodes are popped, a cycle exists -> -1 (self-loops count).
2. dp[v][c] initialised with dp[v][s[v]]=1.
3. Processing u in topo order, for each edge u->v and each letter c: dp[v][c]=max(dp[v][c], dp[u][c] + (s[v]==c)).
4. Answer = max over all dp[v][c].

name: Boris and His Amazing Haircut
tags: constructive algorithms, data structures, dp, dsu, greedy, sortings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0475 Minimum steps to empty array
brief: Arrays a (hair) and b (target); m razors of sizes x, each usable once on a segment setting a_i=min(a_i,x). Decide if a can become b.
key_idea: Need a_i>=b_i; each position with a_i>b_i needs a razor of size exactly b_i, and one razor of size x covers consecutive needing positions with value x unless a larger b in between blocks it (monotonic stack).
solution:
1. If any a_i<b_i -> NO.
2. Scan i with a stack of active razor values (decreasing from bottom): pop while top < b_i (a larger b blocks smaller razors).
3. If a_i>b_i: if top == b_i reuse that razor; else push b_i and need[b_i]++.
4. Count available razors per size (map); if any need[x] > have[x] -> NO, else YES.

need {1:1,2:1} <= have -> YES (matches).

name: Plus and xor
nearest_infosys_question: Q0129 Reduce n to 0 with bit operations
brief: Given A,B (0..2^64-1), find non-negative X,Y with X+Y=A and X xor Y=B, minimizing X; print -1 if impossible.
key_idea: X+Y = (X^Y) + 2(X&Y), so X&Y = (A-B)/2; the minimum X takes only the AND bits.
solution:
1. If A<B or (A-B) odd -> -1.
2. D=(A-B)/2; if D & B != 0 -> -1 (bit can't be in both AND and XOR).
3. X = D, Y = D + B (= A - D).
4. Use unsigned long long for 64-bit range.

name: Magic Tricks
nearest_infosys_question: Q0369 Shortest path (Dijkstra then DP variant)
brief: n balls, special one at position k; m swaps (x_i,y_i) in order, each may be faked (skipped). For every position p, min number of faked swaps so the special ball ends at p, or -1.
key_idea: dist[p] = min skips so far with ball at p; a swap (x,y) only changes dist[x] and dist[y]: perform (ball moves free) or fake (stays, +1).
solution:
1. dist[k]=0, others INF.
2. For each swap (x,y): nx = min(dist[x]+1, dist[y]); ny = min(dist[y]+1, dist[x]); assign simultaneously.
3. Other positions unchanged (a swap not touching p doesn't matter whether faked).
4. Print dist or -1 for INF.

name: Three Blocks Palindrome (hard version)
tags: brute force, data structures, dp, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0061 Longest subarray with sum K
brief: Array (n<=2e5, values<=200). Find the longest subsequence of form [a x times, b y times, a x times] (a may equal b).
key_idea: For outer value a and x, take its x-th occurrence from left and from right; inside, take the most frequent value using prefix counts.
solution: 1) pos[v] = indices of value v; pre[v][i] = count of v in a[0..i). 2) ans = max count of any single value. 3) For each a, for x=1..cnt/2: l=pos[a][x-1], r=pos[a][cnt-x]. 4) inner = max over b of pre[b][r]-pre[b][l+1]; ans=max(ans, 2x+inner). 5) Total work ~ n/2*200.
complexity: O(200 n) time, O(200 n) space

name: Unfair Game
nearest_infosys_question: Q0138 Maximum Xor-Sum in range [0,K]
brief: Multiset has p1 ones, p2 twos, p3 threes, p4 fours (<=200 each). Bob wins a round when XOR of remaining numbers is 0; Eve removes one number per round optimally. Max rounds Bob wins.
key_idea: XOR is 0 iff counts of 4 even and counts of 1,2,3 have equal parity; removing in pairs gives floor(p_i/2) wins per value, plus 1 if p1,p2,p3 are all odd.
solution: 1) XOR=0 iff p4 even and p1,p2,p3 all even or all odd. 2) Eve removes numbers two at a time from the same value, each pair returning to a 'zero' state. 3) Answer = p1/2 + p2/2 + p3/2 + p4/2 + (p1%2 && p2%2 && p3%2 ? 1 : 0).

name: A and B and Interesting Substrings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0072 Subarray sum equals k
brief: Each letter has a value. Count substrings of length >= 2 whose first and last letters are equal and the values of letters strictly between sum to 0.
key_idea: With prefix sums P, a pair i<j works iff s[i]==s[j] and P[j] == P[i+1]; count with a hash map per letter.
solution: 1) P[k] = sum of values of s[0..k-1]. 2) For j=0..n-1 with c=s[j]: ans += cnt[c][P[j]]. 3) Then add key P[j+1] to cnt[c] (as a future left end i=j). 4) Use long long and map/unordered_map per letter.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

name: Eating
tags: binary search, bitmasks, brute force, data structures, dp, greedy, trees, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0142 Max Prefix-XOR Sum of Cyclic Traversal
brief: Slimes w_1..w_n in a line. A query slime x is appended at the right and repeatedly eats its left neighbour if it is not heavier (weight becomes XOR). For each query output how many it eats (independent queries).
key_idea: Slimes with a smaller top bit are always eaten and keep x's top bit; only a slime with top bit >= x's top bit can stop it, and eating such a slime lowers the top bit, so at most 30 jumps per query.
solution:
1. Prefix xor px. For each i and bit b: last[i][b] = largest j<=i with topbit(w_j) >= b (0 if none).
2. Query: cur=x, pos=n. Loop: if cur==0 stop. b=topbit(cur); j=last[pos][b].
3. Eat everything in (j,pos]: cur ^= px[pos]^px[j]. If j==0 -> all eaten, stop.
4. If w_j > cur stop at j (eaten = n-j); else cur ^= w_j, pos = j-1 (top bit decreased).
5. Answer = n - pos at the end.
complexity: O((n + q) * 30) time, O(30 n) space
dry_run:
Sample: w=[1,5,4,11], x=13 (top bit 3).
last[4][3]=4 (11 has bit 3): nothing between; 11<=13 -> cur=6, pos=3.
b=2: last[3][2]=3 (4): 4<=6 -> cur=2, pos=2.
b=1: last[2][1]=2 (5): 5>2 stop. eaten = 4-2 = 2 (matches).

name: Necklace Assembly
tags: brute force, dfs and similar, dp, graphs, greedy, number theory
nearest_infosys_question: Q0509 Playing with MEX
brief: Given n beads (letters) and k, build the longest circular necklace from a subset that is unchanged after rotating by k positions.
key_idea: A length-L necklace invariant under rotation k splits into g = gcd(L,k) cycles of length L/g, each single-coloured.
solution:
1. Count letters cnt[26].
2. For L from n down to 1: g = gcd(L, k), len = L/g.
3. Number of complete cycles we can fill = sum over letters of cnt[c] / len.
4. If that >= g, answer L (first found is max).
5. L=1 always works.

name: Paths on the Tree
tags: dfs and similar, dp, greedy, sortings, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0488 Machine Cooling and Task Scheduling
brief: In a tree rooted at 1, choose k paths that start at the root. Siblings' coverage counts may differ by at most 1. Maximize sum of c_i*s_i, where c_i is how many paths cover vertex i.
key_idea: If cnt paths enter u and u has c children, each child gets cnt/c paths and cnt%c of them get one extra. Each child returns its value plus the gain from one extra path. Give the extras to the children with the largest gains.
solution:
1. dfs(u,cnt) returns {value, gain}. For a leaf: {s_u*cnt, s_u}.
2. Otherwise q=cnt/c, r=cnt%c. Call dfs(v,q) for each child, add up the values, and collect the gains.
3. Sort the gains in descending order. Add the top r gains to the value.
4. gain(u)=s_u+g[r], the next best gain. Answer: dfs(1,k).value.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:

2. Otherwise run a bit DP from the LSB over 62 bits. State (carry, bits of S used <= k, min(S so far, k)). The value is the min number of result 1-bits.
3. At bit b, choose s in {0,1}: tot = n_b + carry + s. The result bit is tot&1 and the new carry is tot>>1.
4. The final state needs carry 0 and the S-so-far value capped at k (meaning S>=k). Answer = popcount(n) + k - best.

name: Clear Symmetry

brief: Given x<=100, find the smallest n such that some n x n 0/1 matrix has exactly x ones, no two ones edge-adjacent, and is symmetric under horizontal and vertical reflection.

2. Otherwise iterate odd n=1,3,5,...: answer is the first n with (n*n+1)/2 >= x.

name: Armchairs
nearest_infosys_question: Q0281 Array Minimization Game
brief: Row of n<=5000 chairs, some occupied (<= n/2). Move people so every initially occupied chair becomes empty; moving i->j costs |i-j|, done sequentially. Minimize total time.
key_idea: Each person goes to a distinct initially-empty chair; optimal matching preserves order, so it's an LCS-like DP over (people, empty chairs).
solution: 1) P = sorted occupied positions, E = sorted empty positions. 2) dp[i][j] = min cost matching first i people using first j empty chairs. 3) dp[0][j]=0; dp[i][j]=min(dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]+|P_i-E_j|); dp[i][j<i]=INF. 4) Answer dp[|P|][|E|].

key_idea: A nice array is a circular partition into equal-valued blocks of length >= 2; blocks of length 2 or 3 suffice (cost |x-y| or max-min), and the block containing index 0 can start at 0, n-1 or n-2.
solution: 1) For rotation r in {0,1,2}: b = a rotated by r. 2) Linear dp: dp[0]=0, dp[i] = min(dp[i-2] + |b[i-1]-b[i-2]|, dp[i-3] + max(b[i-3..i-1]) - min(b[i-3..i-1])), dp[1]=INF. 3) Answer = min over rotations of dp[n]. 4) long long.

name: Shortest Statement Ever
nearest_infosys_question: Q0662 Count pairs A^B<=X with D | A+B
brief: Given x, y < 2^30, find p, q >= 0 with p & q = 0 minimizing |x-p| + |y-q|.

Same for q. 4) Store parent choices to rebuild p, q; answer = min over end states.

solution: 1) solve(v, b): if v empty or b<0 return 0. 2) Split v into zeros/ones by bit b. 3) If one side empty: return solve(other side, b-1). 4) Else return (1<<b) + min(solve(zeros,b-1), solve(ones,b-1)). 5) Answer solve(all, 29).

brief: Sequence of n distinct values (1..n). Count increasing subsequences of length exactly k+1 (k <= 10).

solution: 1) k+1 Fenwick trees over values 1..n. 2) For each a: for len = k+1 down to 2: c = bit[len-1].query(a-1); bit[len].add(a, c). Then bit[1].add(a, 1). 3) Answer = bit[k+1].query(n). 4) Use unsigned long long / long long (answer <= 8e18).

name: MEX Sequences
nearest_infosys_question: Q0310 Minesweeper 1D string completion count
brief: Count the non-empty subsequences x of array a (chosen by index) such that every prefix satisfies |x_i - MEX(prefix)| <= 1. Answer modulo 998244353.
key_idea: A valid sequence is in one of two shapes: d0[m] has MEX m and only values below m; d1[m] has MEX m and also contains m+1. Each new value x changes only a few states.
solution:
1. d0[m]: MEX m, all values < m. d1[m]: MEX m, and m+1 is present.
2. For each x in order:
   d0[x+1] = 2*d0[x+1] + d0[x] (keep x, or extend MEX x up to x+1)
   d1[x+1] *= 2
   if x>=1: d1[x-1] = 2*d1[x-1] + d0[x-1] (jump to MEX+1)
3. New single-element sequences: x=0 adds 1 to d0[1]; x=1 adds 1 to d1[0].
4. Answer = sum of all d0 and d1, mod p.

nearest_infosys_question: Q0381 Graph + DP OA problem
brief: In a D/I/M/A grid, walk to adjacent cells spelling DIMA repeatedly. Output the maximum number of full DIMA passes from any starting D, 'Poor Inna!' if it can be infinite, or 'Poor Dima!' if it is 0.
key_idea: Add an edge from each cell to every neighbour holding the next letter. Any cycle means infinitely many passes, since every cycle goes through a D. Otherwise compute the longest path in nodes with a DP over the topological order. Passes from a D = len/4.

1. Build the implicit edges and their in-degrees.
2. Run Kahn's algorithm. If not every node is processed, print Poor Inna!.

4. '*' cell only state 2; first cell has no prev; last cell cannot be state 1.

name: Number of Subsequences
nearest_infosys_question: Q0328 Vaccine dose scheduling count
brief: String of a,b,c,? (n<=2e5). Over all 3^k replacements of '?', total number of 'abc' subsequences, mod 1e9+7.

name: Hanoi Factory
tags: brute force, data structures, dp, greedy, sortings
nearest_infosys_question: Q0230 Maximum gates taken (2D DP like LIS)
brief: n<=1e5 rings (inner a, outer b, height h). Stack rings so outer radii are non-increasing upward and each ring's outer radius exceeds the inner radius of the ring below. Max total height.
key_idea: Sort by b descending (ties a descending); keep a stack of the current tower; pop rings whose inner radius >= current b, then push with cumulative height.
solution:
1. Sort rings by b desc, then a desc.
2. For each ring x: while stack top's a >= x.b, pop (x would fall through).
3. Height(x) = top's cumulative height (or 0) + h_x; push (x.a, height).
4. Answer = max height seen.
5. Popped rings never help later rings (their b is even smaller).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

name: Pillars
tags: binary search, data structures, dp, sortings, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0320 Stock Trader's Alternating Streak (one mulligan)
brief: Heights h_1..h_n (n<=1e5, h<=1e15). Longest subsequence where consecutive chosen heights differ by at least d; print it.
key_idea: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j<i with h_j <= h_i-d or h_j >= h_i+d: two range-max queries on a segment tree over compressed heights.
solution:
1. Compress heights.
2. For each i: query max (dp, index) on [0, pos(h_i-d)] and [pos(h_i+d), end].
3. dp[i] = best+1, parent = its index; update at pos(h_i).
4. Backtrack from the best i.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Count pairs of positive integers (a,b) with c*lcm(a,b) - d*gcd(a,b) = x (c,d,x <= 1e7, t <= 1e4 tests).
key_idea: Write a=g*p, b=g*q with gcd(p,q)=1: g*(c*p*q - d) = x, so g | x and p*q = (x/g + d)/c; a coprime ordered split of L into p*q has 2^omega(L) ways.
solution:
1. Sieve omega(L) (number of distinct primes) up to 2e7.
2. For each divisor g of x (trial division to sqrt x): s = x/g + d.
3. If c | s: ans += 2^omega(s/c).
4. Print ans.
complexity: O(V log log V) sieve + O(sqrt x) per test

name: Gellyfish and Camellia Japonica
tags: brute force, constructive algorithms, dfs and similar, dp, graphs, greedy, trees
nearest_infosys_question: Q0478 Battery charge to make array strictly increasing
brief: q operations each set c_z = min(c_x, c_y). Given the final array b, find any initial array a (0..1e9) that produces it, or -1.
key_idea: Go backwards keeping lower bounds. After an op, c_z >= need means both c_x and c_y must be >= need beforehand, while the old c_z is free. Choose the minimal bounds as a, then simulate forward to verify.
solution:
1. need = b.
2. For ops from last to first: v=need[z]; need[z]=0; need[x]=max(need[x],v); need[y]=max(need[y],v). Doing it in this order handles z==x or z==y.
3. a = need. Simulate all ops forward on a copy.
4. If the result equals b, print a. Otherwise print -1.

name: Omkar and Circle

4. Use long long.

brief: Find the smallest x >= n (n <= 1e9) that has at most k distinct digits.
key_idea: Repeat: find the first digit index i where the prefix has more than k distinct digits. Add 1 to the number formed by the prefix through i and zero the rest. Stop once the number is k-beautiful. Each step only increases n and skips nothing valid.
solution:
1. s = to_string(n). Scan, adding digits to a set, until the set size exceeds k at index i.

name: Devu and Birthday Celebration
nearest_infosys_question: Q0659 Pick two distinct numbers whose GCD is not prime
brief: q queries (n,f): count ordered ways to write n as f positive parts whose gcd is 1, mod 1e9+7. n,q <= 1e5.
key_idea: Möbius inversion over the common divisor: answer = sum over d|n of mu(d)*C(n/d-1, f-1).
solution:
1. The number of ordered compositions of m into f positive parts is C(m-1, f-1) (stars and bars).
2. Compositions with all parts divisible by d correspond to compositions of n/d.
3. Inclusion-exclusion with Möbius: ans = sum_{d|n} mu(d) C(n/d-1, f-1).
4. Precompute mu with a sieve, divisor lists of squarefree d, and factorials with their inverses.

key_idea: BFS over unordered triples (sorted), about 70^3 states, each with up to 3*n moves, storing parents to print the path.
solution:
1. Encode a state as a sorted triple. BFS from the start.
2. For stone k, the required colour is col[other1][other2]. Move it to any free v with col[s_k][v] equal to that colour.
3. Record the parent and the move (from, to). Stop when {1,2,3} is reached.

name: Sum of Digits
tags: brute force, constructive algorithms, dp, greedy
nearest_infosys_question: Q0478 Battery charge to make array strictly increasing
brief: Find the smallest x >= 0 with f(x)+f(x+1)+...+f(x+k) = n, where f is the digit sum (n<=150, k<=9), or -1.
key_idea: Write x = P, then c nines, then the last digit d. Adding i<=k only carries through the nines, so the total is (k+1)*f(P) + const(c,d). Solve for f(P), build the smallest P with that digit sum (last digit <= 8 so no extra carry), and take the minimum over (c,d).
solution:
1. For c=0..17 and d=0..9: const = sum over i of (d+i<=9 ? 9c+d+i : d+i-10+1).
2. rem = n - const must be >= 0 and divisible by (k+1). s = rem/(k+1).
3. P = the smallest number with digit sum s and last digit <= 8: last = min(8,s), then the remainder as (r, 9, 9, ...) in front.
4. Candidate x = P + c nines + d (strip leading zeros). Keep the numerically smallest (compare by length, then lexicographically). (Brute-force verified.)

name: Koa and the Beach (Hard Version)
nearest_infosys_question: Q0478 Battery charge to make array strictly increasing
brief: Koa crosses n sea cells; at time t depth at i is d_i + p[t mod 2k] where p rises 0..k then falls to 1. Each second she moves forward or waits; depth must stay <= l where she stands. Can she reach the island?
key_idea: Cells with d_i + k <= l are safe forever and reset the state to 'tide k, falling'; between them simulate greedily: while falling wait as needed (tide = min(tide-1, l-d_i)), while rising you must keep moving.
solution:
1. tide = k, down = true at the shore.
2. Safe cell (d+k <= l): reset tide=k, down=true.
3. If d_i > l -> No.
4. If down: tide = min(tide-1, l-d_i) (waiting earlier is free since water falls); if tide <= 0 set tide=0, down=false.
5. If rising: tide++; if tide > l-d_i -> No.
6. Finish -> Yes.

Cell 2: d+k=1 <= l safe -> reset.

name: Fancy Stack
nearest_infosys_question: Q0328 Vaccine dose scheduling count
brief: Count arrangements b of the multiset a (n even, n <= 5000) with b1 < b2 > b3 < b4 > ... < bn and b2 < b4 < ... < bn, mod 998244353.
key_idea: Even positions are increasing peaks p_1 < ... < p_k; odd slot 1 needs a value < p_1 and slot i+1 needs < p_i. Process distinct values in decreasing order with state j = #peaks chosen: a peak opens a slot for smaller values, other copies fill already-open slots (C(free, copies)).
solution:
1. Group equal values, process descending; processed = #elements already handled.
2. opened(j) = max(0, j-1) + [j == k] (the last peak p_1 opens two slots); free = opened(j) - (processed - j).
3. Not a peak: dp[j] * C(free, c).
4. One copy becomes the next peak: dp[j+1] += dp[j] * C(free, c-1) (copies must use slots of larger peaks).
5. Answer dp[k] after all values.

name: Trails (Hard)
nearest_infosys_question: Q0329 Ordered coin change count with large target
brief: m <= 1e5 cabins with s_i short and l_i long trails to a lake. For n <= 1e9 days, go cabin -> lake -> cabin, with at least one short trail per day, starting at cabin 1. Count trail sequences mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: T[i][j] = s_i s_j + s_i l_j + l_i s_j = t_i t_j - l_i l_j (t = s + l) has rank 2: T = A B^T with A = [t, l], B = [t, -l]. Then T^n = A (B^T A)^{n-1} B^T, a 2x2 matrix power.
solution:
1. Compute tt = t.t, tl = t.l, ll = l.l, St = sum t, Sl = sum l.
2. C = [[tt, tl], [-tl, -ll]].
3. R = C^{n-1} by fast exponentiation.

name: Antichain
nearest_infosys_question: Q0456 Minimum jumps to reach end of array
brief: An acyclic orientation of a cycle of n <= 1e6 vertices (edge i between i and i+1 mod n, direction given by s_i). Find the maximum antichain.
key_idea: Maximal runs of same-direction edges are chains, and adjacent runs share an endpoint (a source or sink). An interior vertex (run length >= 2) blocks one run; an endpoint blocks two. So answer = #long runs + the sum over maximal blocks of consecutive length-1 runs of floor(len/2) (all short: floor(k/2)).
solution:
1. Rotate to a run boundary and split the cycle into run lengths.
2. Count the runs of length >= 2.
3. If none: print k/2.
4. Else start at a long run, walk cyclically, and add floor(block/2) for each block of short runs.

name: Palindromic Doubles
nearest_infosys_question: Q0320 Stock Trader's Alternating Streak (one mulligan)
brief: Sequence (n <= 2.5e5) where each value appears at most twice. Find the length of the longest palindromic subsequence.
key_idea: A palindrome is a chain of nested equal-value pairs (l1 < l2 < ... < r2 < r1) plus an optional middle element. Process pairs by increasing l; f = 1 + the max f among earlier pairs with a larger r (BIT on reversed r). Add 1 if the innermost pair has a gap (r - l > 1).
solution:
1. For each value seen twice record (l, r).
2. Scan l = 1..n; for a pair: f = 1 + max f over r' > r (prefix max BIT on n+1-r).
3. ans = max(ans, 2f + (r - l > 1)), with ans starting at 1.
4. Update the BIT at r with f.

nearest_infosys_question: Q0448 Paper Sheets (Minimum Folds)
brief: Need n planks of length 18, n of 21 and n of 25; standard planks have length 60 and can be cut but not joined. Find the minimum number of 60-planks (n <= 1000).
key_idea: A plank holding a 25 fits at most 2 pieces (25+18+18=61>60); others fit 3 pieces only as 18+18+18, 18+18+21 or 18+21+21. Lower bound and construction both give ceil(7n/6).
solution:

2. 18s and 21s: n/2 planks of (18,21,21) and the rest as (18,18,18) -> 2n/3 planks.
3. Bound: 3n pieces <= 3*P - (#planks with a 25) and that count >= n/2, so P >= 7n/6.
4. Answer = (7n+5)/6 (integer ceil).

name: DZY Loves Sequences
nearest_infosys_question: Q0215 Paint House with Budget Constraint
brief: Given a sequence (n <= 1e5), find the longest contiguous subsegment that can be made strictly increasing by changing at most one element.
key_idea: L[i] = increasing run ending at i, R[i] = increasing run starting at i. Changing a[i] joins L[i-1] and R[i+1] when a[i+1] - a[i-1] >= 2; otherwise you can still extend one side by 1.
solution:
1. Compute L and R (strictly increasing runs).
2. ans = max over i of L[i-1] + 1 and R[i+1] + 1 (change a[i] to extend one run), capped by n.
3. If 0 < i < n-1 and a[i+1] - a[i-1] >= 2: ans = max(ans, L[i-1] + 1 + R[i+1]).
4. n = 1 -> 1.

name: Rudolf and k Bridges
tags: binary search, data structures, dp, two pointers
nearest_infosys_question: Q0274 Maximum sum subset with index gap between a and b
brief: An n x m river grid has depths a[i][j] (banks a[i][1]=a[i][m]=0). A support at (i,j) costs a[i][j]+1; a bridge in a row needs supports at columns 1 and m with at most d empty cells between consecutive supports. Build bridges on k consecutive rows with minimum total cost.
key_idea: Per row, dp[j]=a[j]+1+min(dp[j-d-1..j-1]) using a monotonic deque; then minimum sliding sum of k consecutive row costs.
solution:
1. For each row: dp[1]=1; for j>1, dp[j]=a[j]+1+min dp[t] for t in [j-d-1, j-1] (gap |j-t|-1<=d).
2. Maintain that window minimum with a monotonic deque of indices (pop front if index < j-d-1, pop back while dp[back]>=dp[j]).
3. cost[row]=dp[m]; use long long (up to 2e5*1e6).
4. Answer = min over i of cost[i]+...+cost[i+k-1] (prefix sums or sliding window).

name: Cirno and Number (Hard Version)

nearest_infosys_question: Q0498 Make Equal Elements Adjacent (min adjacent swaps)
brief: Given a (0<=a<=1e17) and an increasing set of allowed digits d (1..10 digits), find the minimum |a-b| over non-negative integers b written only with allowed digits.
key_idea: The best b is either a itself, or the closest smaller/larger number of the same length obtained by matching a prefix of a and then deviating, or the largest shorter / smallest longer number.
solution:
1. Let A = decimal string of a, L = its length.
2. Same length: walk positions p while A[0..p-1] are all allowed; at p try the largest allowed digit < A[p] followed by max digit (no leading zero if L>1), and the smallest allowed digit > A[p] followed by min digit. If all digits allowed, b = a.
3. Shorter: L-1 copies of the max digit (if L>1 and max digit > 0); also b=0 if 0 is allowed.
4. Longer: smallest non-zero allowed digit followed by L copies of the min digit.
5. Answer = min |a-b| over candidates; use __int128 (19-digit candidates overflow long long).

2. smin[i], smax[i] = min/max of p[j]-p[i] for j in [i..n] (includes 0), computed right to left.
3. Query: base=p[l-1]; lo=min(pmin[l-1], base+smin[r]); hi=max(pmax[l-1], base+smax[r]).
4. Answer hi-lo+1 (steps are +-1 so all values in between are hit).

nearest_infosys_question: Q0092 Array AP Queries
brief: Grid of '.'/'X'; a cell is exitable if you can leave the grid moving only up/left through empty cells. For queries of column ranges [x1,x2], decide if the exitability pattern of that subgrid uniquely determines the grid.
key_idea: Ambiguity arises exactly when some cell has 'X' above it and 'X' to its left; mark column j bad if g[i-1][j]=='X' and g[i][j-1]=='X', then a query is NO iff a bad column lies in (x1, x2].
solution:
1. For each column j>=2 (1-indexed), bad[j]=1 if some row i>=2 has g[i-1][j]=='X' and g[i][j-1]=='X'.
2. Such a cell is non-exitable whether empty or filled -> undeterminable, and only if both blockers are inside the range (columns j-1 and j).
3. Prefix sums P over bad.
4. Query: YES iff P[x2]-P[x1]==0 (column x1 itself has its left neighbor outside the range).
